newsitem.title: ITALY: Ciampi says does not expect Italy mini-budget.
newsitem.headline: Ciampi says does not expect Italy mini-budget.

text.p: Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said on Tuesday he did not think the government would have to resort to a mini-budget next year after its 62.5 trillion lire main package, but would weigh up the situation.
"I don't think we'll get it wrong," he told a news conference. "If there is a need for an additional budget, the government will take note."

Ciampi's remarks came after the International Monetary Fund forecast in a report late on Monday that Prime Minister Romano Prodi's 1997 austerity budget would not be enough to guarantee membership of a single European currency planned for 1999.
The IMF said in the report, published following a recent visit to Italy by IMF experts, that the government needed to crack down on state spending.
"We call for the definition, as early as possible in 1997, of durable cost-saving measures affecting spending on social security, health and public employment," it said.
It said a big corrective package could be needed early next year to meet the goals set down in the Maastricht Treaty for single currency membership.
Ciampi welcomed evaluations on the Italian economy by the IMF, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and the European Commission.
"All three are comforting in the sense that (they say) the line the government has chosen is correct," he said.

All three have said Italy would need a mini-budget next year to meet current government economic goals. The IMF suggested in Monday's report that a mini-budget package of up to 13-14 trillion lire could be needed early next year.
"Even the amount (of such a mini-budget) is comforting because...although it is a large amount it is certainly bearable."
